title: The Angle It Cannot Hold: Joint Limits and the Reachable Set

questions.question: An arm's shoulder can turn from -0.6 to 2.2 rad and its elbow from -2.4 to 2.4. Compared with the workspace its links alone allow, how much can it still reach?
options: About 55 percent, and the part it loses is not all around the outside
About 95 percent: limits only shave the extremes off
All of it, more slowly, since it can always fold a different way
About 20 percent, since two limits multiply
questions.explanation: Measured on a 1 cm grid, 13878 of 25140 geometrically reachable cells survive. The lost region includes ordinary points in the middle of the reach, which is why refused targets look scattered rather than edge-like.

questions.question: A shoulder is limited to [-0.6, 2.2] rad. The solver returns -6.10 rad. Can the arm hold that pose?
options: Yes: -6.10 and 0.183 are the same direction, and 0.183 is inside the range
No: -6.10 is below -0.6
Only if the joint is allowed to turn more than once
It depends on which way the arm turns to get there
questions.explanation: An angle is a direction, not a quantity. -6.10 plus one full turn is 0.183. The comparison has to happen after the turns come off, and a solver that builds angles from a difference of two atan2 calls produces values across roughly (-2pi, 2pi) as a matter of course.

questions.question: That same shoulder is asked to point at -3.0 rad, which is genuinely illegal. Clamping the number gives -0.6. What does clamping it as an angle give, and why?
options: 2.2, because measured as an angle the far end is 1.08 rad away and -0.6 is 2.4 rad away
-0.6, the same answer: clamping is clamping
0.0, the midpoint of the range
-3.0 unchanged, since neither end is close
questions.explanation: Going the other way round the circle is shorter. A number clamp cannot see that, because it compares magnitudes rather than directions, and on six illegal directions it picked the further end three times.

questions.question: The solver returns the elbow-up answer, the limits refuse it, and the code clamps both joint angles into range. How far can the tool end up from the target on a 0.9 m arm?
options: Up to about 0.73 m, and usually the target was reachable by the other elbow
At most the amount each joint was clamped by, in radians times the link length
Close: clamping only moves the joint as far as it has to
It cannot be measured, because the pose is invalid
questions.explanation: The two joint angles are not independent. Moving the shoulder and leaving the elbow where the old solution put it answers a question nobody asked. On the four measured targets the clamped error ran from 0.14 to 0.73 m, and on three of them the other branch was exact.

questions.question: nearest_reachable scans only the elbow, not both joints. Why is that not an approximation?
options: For a fixed elbow the tool sits at a fixed radius, so the best shoulder is the target's bearing minus the arm's own offset, clamped as an angle
It is an approximation, traded for speed
Because the shoulder limit is wider than the elbow limit
Because the elbow contributes more to the tool position than the shoulder does
questions.explanation: The shoulder is solved rather than searched, so it is exact for every elbow sample. Against a 601 by 601 grid over both joints, on eight targets, the scan was never worse and used 16008 evaluations against 2889608.

questions.question: Your solver reports it got within 4 mm of a target the arm cannot reach. What must the test check before you believe it?
options: That the pose it returned is legal and actually lands 4 mm away
That 4 mm is under the tolerance the application needs
That the same target fails on a second machine
That the scan used enough steps
questions.explanation: A function that reports a distance it did not achieve is worse than one that fails, because nothing downstream can tell. A stub returning distance 0 passed four of this lesson's checks until the suite recomputed the distance from the returned joint angles.
